facts.claim: Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia marriage page: the rite is performed by a Priest before a covered ceremonial table in the middle of the Soleas, in front of the Holy Altar; on it are the Holy Gospel, a cup of wine, the betrothal rings and the wedding crowns. Two candles are lit as a reminder that Christ is 'the Light of the world'. The groom stands on the right and the bride on the left.
Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: the ceremony has two parts, the Betrothal Service with the blessing of the rings, and the Marriage Service with the crowning of the bride and groom.

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: every Orthodox betrothal is a double ring ceremony; the Priest blesses each partner with the rings three times, the rings are placed on the fourth finger of the right hand, and the koumbaros (best man) exchanges them, over and under, three times.

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: the Marriage Service is called 'stepsis' in Greek, meaning crowning. The Priest joins the right hands of the bride and groom, which stay joined for the rest of the service, symbolising the 'oneness' of the couple.

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: the crowning is the climax of the Marriage Service; the crowns are a sign of the bond between bride and groom and represent the glory and honour God bestows on the couple. Crowns were usually plaited of lemon blossoms or flowers; today they are often silver or gold. The Best Man exchanges the crowns three times while the Priest and Chanter sing 'Lord our God, crown them in glory and honour.'
Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: the readings are the Epistle from St Paul's Letter to the Ephesians 5:20-33 and the Gospel from John 2:1-11.

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: in remembrance of Christ's first miracle at Cana, a cup of wine is shared by the bride and groom as a sign of unity with each other and with Christ. It is not Holy Communion but a symbol of the 'common cup of life', the mutual sharing of joy and sorrow. The Priest offers it first to the groom, then the bride.

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: the Dance of Isaiah is a procession in a circle, a symbolic dance for the joy of God's presence, led by the Priest holding the Holy Gospel, while the Priest and Chanter sing 'Rejoice, Isaiah'.

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: after the procession the Priest blesses the groom and bride and removes the crowns during a prayer; before congratulating the newlyweds he separates their right hands with the Holy Gospel, signifying that nothing and no one except God should come between the couple.

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: the Church allows people to divorce and remarry but no more than two times; second and third weddings are usually not considered sacraments, and their prayers have a penitential character.

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: weddings are performed by a Priest recognised as canonical by the Archdiocese; the laws and regulations for weddings are set by the Holy Canons of the Orthodox Church and implemented by the Archdiocese, and apply to every Greek Orthodox Priest across Australia.

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: there must be no impediment by relationship under the Canons of the Church and civil law; the page lists prohibited marriages, including between parents and children or grandchildren, brothers-in-law and sisters-in-law, uncles or aunts and nieces or nephews, first cousins, foster relationships, godparents and godchildren (or godchildren's parents), and godchildren of the same godparent.

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: the koumbaros or koumbara is usually Orthodox; non-Orthodox Christians of an acceptable denomination may stand as best man or matron of honour at the wedding, but may not become godparents at the couple's children's christenings.

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: a marriage cannot take place in the Orthodox Church between an Orthodox Christian and a non-Christian; the non-Orthodox partner must belong to a Christian denomination acceptable to the Orthodox Church (the page lists them, including Roman Catholic, Anglican, Uniting, Lutheran and Presbyterian, and lists denominations whose members may not marry in the Church). A baptism performed by a female pastor or member of clergy is not accepted.

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: having been baptised in the name of the Holy Trinity, both parties are asked to declare that any children will be baptised in the Eastern Orthodox Church and raised in the Orthodox Faith.

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: people who are not Christian or were never baptised can only marry in the Orthodox Church after being baptised in a denomination acceptable to the Orthodox Church. A non-Orthodox spouse does not become a member of the Church and may not receive Holy Communion; non-Orthodox clergy may not co-celebrate.

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: where both parties are Greek Orthodox, they must have been baptised in a canonical Orthodox Church; people baptised in a non-canonical church must first speak to a canonical Priest. Marriages with members of Oriental Orthodox Churches (for example Coptic, Syrian, Armenian, Indian Orthodox) are permitted.

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: marriages are not permitted from 13 December until Christmas Day; on 5 January (eve of Epiphany); from Great Lent until Easter Sunday (dates vary each year); from 1 to 15 August (Dormition of the Theotokos); on 29 August; and on 14 September.

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: on the day, the groom and groomsmen should arrive at least 15 minutes before the service and the bride's party at least 5 minutes before; the custom of the bride arriving late is not based on any religious tradition. Without the rings and the crowns, the wedding cannot commence.

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: every Greek Orthodox Priest in Australia is also a registered civil celebrant, authorised to conduct the marriage under both State and Ecclesiastical law, but may perform the civil marriage only together with the religious service on the same day.

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: the Notice of Intended Marriage (for the Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages) and the Application to the Archdiocese must be completed in the presence of the Priest at least one calendar month before the wedding, preferably three months. The Parish Priest gives directions on documents and on Archdiocese and local church fees, which vary by circumstances.

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: both parties must present a birth certificate (if born in Australia) or passport (if born overseas) and a baptismal certificate; Orthodox parties never married before need a Certificate of Celibacy ('Agamias') from their local parish priest, signed by two witnesses. Widowed parties provide the spouse's death certificate.

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: divorcing parties need a civil divorce certificate and then an ecclesiastical divorce; for a second or third marriage, both divorces must be issued at least one calendar month before the next marriage.

insider_details.detail: Plan the ceremony as two moves: the betrothal at the back of the church (narthex) and then a procession to the centre for the crowning, per the Orthodox Church in America service text. Brief the photographer and videographer to cover both positions.
Wedding bands go on the right hand in the Orthodox rite (OCA service text). Tell the jeweller and the couple so rings are sized for the right hand.

The procession three times around the table (to 'Rejoice, O Isaiah!') has the groomsmen following and holding the crowns (OCA text). Rehearse it with the sponsors so they know their place and the photographer gets clear sightlines.
Ask the parish which readings are used. The OCA text sets Ephesians 5:20-33 and John 2:1-12; couples who want a bilingual booklet for Australian guests can print these.
